newsitem.title: USA: Actress Pamela Lee wins breach-of-contract lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: Actress Pamela Lee wins breach-of-contract lawsuit.

text.p: Former "Baywatch" TV star Pamela Anderson Lee, who had been sued for $5 million by a movie production company, did not break any contract when she backed out of a film deal, a judge ruled on Tuesday.

In a written judgment, Judge David Horowitz said the filmmakers, The Private Movie Co., failed to prove "by a preponderance of evidence" that Lee entered into a contract to make the cable TV movie "Hello, She Lied."
"The plaintiff presented no evidence that Lee personally agreed to perform in the film," the judge wrote.

He said his ruling in favour of Lee was also based on the fact that neither side could agree on the definition of 'simlated sex' and that the plaintiff failed to provide concrete evidence it had lost money over Lee's withdrawal.
The verdict was made available to both parties and to the media. None of the parties appeared in court on Tuesday and there was no immediate comment from either side.
In his ruling, Horowitz said there was no binding agreement, despite the producer's claim that she had made an oral agreement to make the film.
During the non-jury trial, lawyers for the plaintiffs also acknowledged that a written agreement with Lee had never been executed.
The company had sued her for $5 million, claiming she broke a contract because she was offered a better deal to make a feature film, "Barb Wire."
The actress, who is married to rock drummer Tommy Lee of Motley Crue, said during testimony this month that she pulled out of the project because she objected to sex scenes in the proposed film.

The moviemakers, who claimed to have lost millions of dollars as a result of Lee backing out, later made the film as "Miami Hustler" with model Kathy Ireland in the lead role. Ireland had a no-nudity clause in her contract.

The Canadian-born Lee, who attended every day of the trial, told the court during her testimony that although she was not opposed to nudity, she objected to certain graphic scenes involving simulated sex in "Hello, She Lied."
In one session in Los Angeles County Court, Lee read from the proposed script, describing in detail what sex acts she would have been required to perform on camera.
She said that even when she requested changes in the script, the producers still required her to simulate sex acts in a shower scene and on a pool table.
As a result of a previous bad experience in a film involving simulated love-making, Lee said: "I don't want to be touched by people I don't know. I have that right."
In his ruling, Judge Horowitz wrote: "the parties do not and did not agree on the definition of 'simulated sex.'

"It is obvious the deal-point relating to simulated sex scenes was not resolved," he wrote. "When she received and reviewed the script, she determined that it contained several scenes of simulated sex and decided not to do the film."

The plaintiffs argued that Lee's objections to sex scenes were just excuses and that the real reason she backed out of the film was because she was offered $500,000 to make "Barb Wire" as opposed to $200,000 for "Hello, She Lied."
